title.en: Saying who you are responsible for

summary.en: A present statement, a preposition and an everyday relative clause.

body.en:
Malik says *أنا مسؤول عن كل الناس اللي برا*: I am responsible for all the people outside. In the source scene, those people are beyond the meeting room; the line does not say that everybody is out in the street.

*أنا* is the independent pronoun I. It goes directly before the adjective *مسؤول*, responsible. This affirmative present statement does not need a separate word matching English am. This is a statement pattern; it does not mean Arabic never uses verbs corresponding to be.

*مسؤول* is masculine singular because Malik is describing himself. A woman describing herself uses the feminine form shown in the drawer. The preposition *عن* introduces the people or matter for which someone is responsible.

*كل الناس* means all the people. The definite article is attached to the noun in *الناس*, so it remains part of one selectable written word. The phrase *اللي برا* then describes which people he means. In this everyday Saudi sentence, *اللي* is an invariant relative marker. Formal written Arabic has a different relative-pronoun paradigm; this lesson is not teaching one form for every variety of Arabic.

The [Cairo Academy entry for the question/accountability family](https://www.arabicacademy.gov.eg/ar/search_engine/roots/سأل) documents the link between being responsible and having to answer for something.
